question: A flying bar needs to carry a scenic piece and two performers standing on a truss below it. What factors would you want to understand before that's signed off as safe?
lookingFor: Understanding that rigging safety is a chain of calculations and checks, not a gut call, and that the applicant knows to defer to a qualified rigger.

bullets: Mention the need for a safe working load calculation covering the combined weight plus a safety factor, not just the static weight
Recognise that a chartered rigger or technical manager, not the applicant, makes the final sign-off
Show awareness of inspection, certification, and rehearsal of the move before it goes anywhere near a live audience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to know the safe working load of the bar and every piece of hardware in the chain, because it's not just the scenery's weight, it's the performers plus a proper safety margin on top. I'd never sign that off myself, I'd want it calculated and certified by a qualified rigger and checked against current inspection records. I'd also want the move rehearsed slowly and observed before it's run at speed with people underneath it, because the theory can look fine on paper and still surprise you in the room.

commonMistakes: Guessing at a safety margin instead of naming that a professional calculates it
Treating it as purely a technical question and ignoring the people standing under the load
Assuming a rehearsal run isn't necessary once the paperwork is signed
followUps: Who in a production team is actually responsible for that sign-off?

subtopic: Fire safety and means of escape
question: Why do theatres have such strict rules about the width of aisles and the number of exits, and what happens when a production wants to add extra seating or staging that eats into that space?
lookingFor: Grasp of licensing basics and the instinct to treat audience safety limits as non-negotiable even under creative or commercial pressure.

bullets: Explain that exit widths and aisle counts are calculated against occupancy to guarantee an evacuation time
Note that a venue's safe capacity is licensed and can't be quietly stretched for a bigger house
Show the right instinct: extra seating or staging has to go back to the licensing authority, not get squeezed in unofficially
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Those widths aren't arbitrary, they're calculated so that everyone in the building can get out safely within a set time even in the worst case, so they're tied directly to how many people the venue is licensed to hold. If a production wanted more seats or a bigger stage footprint, my instinct is that's a conversation with the venue's licensing and safety officer before it's a design decision, not after. I'd rather lose some seats than be the person who quietly narrowed an escape route because the show needed the space.

commonMistakes: Treating capacity limits as a suggestion rather than a legal requirement
Not knowing that changes to seating or staging need re-approval
Focusing only on the artistic upside without mentioning the safety trade-off
followUps: Who would you go to first if a director asked for extra staging that blocked an aisle?

question: How does designing for sightlines change when you move from a proscenium arch to theatre in the round?
lookingFor: Practical understanding that staging decisions ripple through set, lighting, and blocking depending on where the audience physically sits.

bullets: Explain that proscenium sightlines mostly worry about masking and depth from one direction
Note that in the round, every side is a front row, so scenery, rigging, and even actors' backs become visible problems
Connect this to knock-on effects for lighting angles and blocking choices, not just set design
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In a proscenium you're mostly protecting one dominant sightline, masking the wings and worrying about how much depth reads from the stalls to the back row. In the round there's no backstage to hide in, every seat is a front seat from some angle, so scenery has to work in silhouette from all sides and you lose the option of a painted flat that only needs to look good from one direction. It also changes lighting, because you can't hide a rig above the stage without it being visible, and it changes blocking, because a performer's back is someone's front row view for a good chunk of the show.

commonMistakes: Treating sightlines as only a lighting or only a set design issue
Assuming in-the-round staging is just proscenium staging shrunk down
Forgetting that blocking has to account for audience on every side
followUps: What would you do differently for a thrust stage compared to both of those?

subtopic: Calling a show from the book
question: What does it actually mean to 'call' a show, and why is a good prompt book so important to getting it right?
lookingFor: Understanding of the deputy/stage manager's live coordination role and why precise, legible cue documentation is what makes a show repeatable.

bullets: Explain that calling means giving live 'standby' and 'go' instructions over headset to cue lighting, sound, and moves in real time
Describe the prompt book as the master script marked with every cue, so the show runs the same way every night
Note the pressure of doing this live, and why clarity and consistency in marking cues matters more than personal shorthand
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Calling a show means sitting with the script during the live performance and giving the standby and go cues over headset so lighting, sound, and any automated moves land at exactly the right line or moment. The prompt book is what makes that repeatable, it's the master copy of the script with every single cue marked precisely, so the show comes out the same whether it's press night or a Tuesday matinee with an understudy on. What struck me learning about it is how much pressure sits with one calm, clear voice, because a cue called a beat late can throw off an actor's rhythm or miss a scene change entirely.

commonMistakes: Confusing 'calling' with directing or blocking the show
Not mentioning consistency across performances as the point of the prompt book
Underestimating how much live judgement the role requires
followUps: What would you do if you lost your place in the book mid-cue?

question: A venue is running two different productions in rep, alternating nights on the same stage. What's actually involved in making that changeover work?
lookingFor: Awareness that repertory staging is a logistics and storage problem as much as a creative one, requiring meticulous planning.

bullets: Explain that rep means striking one show's set, lighting, and props and resetting another's within a tight window, often overnight
Mention practical needs: labelled storage, a strict get-out and get-in schedule, and lighting/sound states that can be recalled quickly
Show awareness that this demands close coordination across every department, not just stage management
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Running two shows in rep means that overnight, or sometimes between a matinee and an evening show, the crew has to fully strike one set and lighting rig and reset a completely different one, so nothing can be left to memory. In practice that means everything has to be labelled and stored so it can go back exactly where it was, lighting and sound states saved so they can be recalled rather than reprogrammed from scratch, and a schedule tight enough that everyone knows their exact task and order. What I find compelling about it is that it's really a logistics discipline as much as a creative one, the artistry only survives if the changeover is boringly reliable.

commonMistakes: Assuming rep scheduling is just 'doing two shows' with no mention of the changeover logistics
Ignoring the storage and labelling problem
Focusing only on set and forgetting lighting and sound states also need resetting
followUps: How would you handle it if the changeover overran and the next show's get-in was delayed?

question: A touring production is arriving at a venue that's smaller than the one the show was designed for, with a lower grid height. What's your process for adapting?
lookingFor: Problem-solving that starts from the technical rider and prioritises what's essential to preserve versus what can flex.

bullets: Start from the technical rider and the venue's own specifications, checked well before load-in day
Identify what's essential to the show's storytelling versus what's a nice-to-have and can be cut or simplified
Show collaborative problem-solving with the venue's technical staff rather than assuming the original design just has to fit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by comparing the show's technical rider against the venue's actual specs as early as possible, ideally weeks before load-in rather than discovering the mismatch on the day. Then I'd sit with the director and designers to work out what's genuinely essential to the storytelling, a key flying effect maybe, versus what was just how it happened to be built for the original venue and can be adapted. I'd also want to be talking to the venue's own technical staff early, because they know that grid and that stage better than anyone touring in, and a good adaptation is usually a collaboration rather than the touring team just cutting things unilaterally.

commonMistakes: Assuming the show has to be performed identically regardless of venue constraints
Leaving the comparison against venue specs until load-in day
Not involving the venue's own technical staff in solving the problem
followUps: What would you cut first if you genuinely couldn't fit everything?

question: What are the trade-offs between using automated, motorised scenery and doing scene changes manually with a crew?
lookingFor: Ability to weigh cost, reliability, speed, and creative flexibility rather than assuming automation is simply 'better'.

bullets: Note automation's advantages: speed, precision, repeatability, and fewer crew needed on stage during a change
Note the trade-offs: cost, the need for specialist maintenance, and the risk when it fails mid-performance
Show judgement about when manual changes are actually the more reliable or more theatrical choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Automation can make a scene change fast, silent, and exactly repeatable every night, which matters hugely for a complex show, and it also reduces how many crew need to be on a dark stage during a change, which is a safety win. But it's expensive to install and maintain, needs specialist technicians on call, and when it fails mid-show you can be stuck in a way a manual crew can usually improvise around. I think the honest answer is that automation earns its cost when the move is genuinely too complex or too fast for people to do safely, but for a lot of shows a well-drilled crew doing a manual change is cheaper, more flexible, and just as reliable.

commonMistakes: Treating automation as automatically superior with no downside
Ignoring the cost and maintenance burden
Not considering failure scenarios mid-performance
followUps: How would you plan for what happens if an automated element fails during a live show?

question: How does choosing a gel colour actually affect what an audience feels, beyond just making the stage brighter or dimmer?
lookingFor: Genuine grasp of how colour temperature and saturation shape mood and skin tone, not just a vocabulary list.

bullets: Explain that colour affects mood and atmosphere, warm tones reading as comforting or nostalgic, cool tones as clinical or tense
Mention the practical issue of how gels interact with skin tone and costume colour, not just the set
Show awareness that colour choices have to serve the story and the director's intent, not just look striking in isolation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A warm amber wash can make the exact same scene feel nostalgic or safe, while a cold blue in the same spot can make it feel isolating or tense, even if the actors and blocking don't change at all. It's not just about the set either, gels interact with skin tone and costume colour in ways that can flatter or completely wash someone out, so I'd want to test it on the actual performers, not just on paper. What I find genuinely interesting is that colour is one of the few tools that talks to the audience almost subconsciously, so the choice has to serve what the story needs emotionally in that moment, not just what looks striking as a standalone image.

commonMistakes: Talking only about brightness or visibility, missing the emotional dimension
Ignoring the effect on skin tone and costume
Choosing colour for visual impact without tying it to story or mood
followUps: Can you think of a moment in a production you've seen where lighting colour did real emotional work?

question: What's the difference between sound reinforcement and sound design, and why does mixing them up cause problems?
lookingFor: Precise understanding of two related but distinct disciplines, and why conflating them leads to poor decisions on a production.

bullets: Define reinforcement as making sure the audience can hear the actors clearly, mics, speakers, levels
Define design as the creative use of sound, effects, music, atmosphere, to tell the story
Explain the practical consequence: a great design badly reinforced is inaudible, and great reinforcement with no design is flat
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sound reinforcement is the technical job of making sure the audience can actually hear what's happening on stage, so mic choice, speaker placement, and levels so dialogue doesn't get swallowed by the room. Sound design is the creative layer on top, the chosen effects, underscoring, and atmosphere that help tell the story, which could be anything from a rumble of thunder to a barely audible hum that builds tension. The reason mixing them up causes problems is that a brilliant design is worthless if it's poorly reinforced and the audience can't hear the dialogue clearly, and technically flawless reinforcement with no design thinking behind it just sounds correct but says nothing.

commonMistakes: Using the terms interchangeably without a clear definition
Treating sound as purely technical with no creative dimension
Ignoring the practical consequence of getting the balance wrong
followUps: Who typically holds each of those responsibilities on a production team?

subtopic: Working with an intimacy or fight coordinator
question: Why have intimacy and fight coordinators become a more standard part of production teams, and what does good collaboration with them look like from a production standpoint?
lookingFor: Awareness of a genuine shift in industry practice, and understanding of the coordinator's role as both safety and craft.

bullets: Explain the shift: intimacy and fight work used to be left to directors and actors to improvise, and that led to real harm and inconsistency
Describe the coordinator's role as choreographing repeatable, consented, physically safe sequences, not just supervising
Show what good production support looks like: rehearsal time, private space, and taking their safety calls as final
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a long time intimate scenes and stage combat were often just worked out between the director and the actors on the spot, which meant inconsistent choreography and, in plenty of documented cases, real discomfort or harm that nobody had a structured way to raise. A coordinator's job is to choreograph those moments the same way a fight director choreographs a sword fight, movement by movement, so it's repeatable, consented to in advance, and physically safe every single time it's performed. From a production standpoint, supporting that well means actually giving them dedicated rehearsal time and a private space rather than squeezing it into a general rehearsal, and treating their safety calls as final the way you would a rigger's.

commonMistakes: Treating the coordinator as an optional extra rather than a safety-critical role
Assuming this is only relevant to intimate scenes and not stage combat
Not mentioning consent and repeatability as the actual point of the choreography
followUps: What would you do if a director wanted to skip a scheduled intimacy rehearsal to save time?

question: What goes into making sure a show can go on when a lead performer is suddenly unwell?
lookingFor: Understanding that cover systems require ongoing rehearsal and technical adaptation, not just a name on a cast list.

bullets: Explain that understudies need to be rehearsed regularly, not just cast and forgotten about
Mention the technical side: costumes, mic packs, and blocking sometimes need adjusting for a different performer
Show awareness of the communication chain, who decides, how fast, and how the audience and cast are told
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's not enough to just have someone officially down as the understudy, they need actual rehearsal time built into the schedule so the choreography, blocking, and any tricky cues are genuinely in their body, not just watched from the wings. There's a technical side too, a costume or a mic pack fitted for one performer might need quick adjusting for another, and any partner-dependent blocking, a lift or a fight sequence, needs to have been rehearsed with that specific cover. And there needs to be a clear, fast decision chain for the night itself, who makes the call, how quickly the crew and box office are told, because a late call with no plan is how a show actually falls apart.

commonMistakes: Assuming understudies are ready simply because they've been cast
Forgetting the technical adjustments, costume, mics, blocking, that a swap requires
Not addressing the decision and communication chain on the actual night
followUps: How much rehearsal time do you think an understudy realistically needs before opening?

question: Theatre has traditionally built sets from new timber and materials that often get skipped after a short run. What's changing about that, and where do you think production departments should draw the line between sustainability and what a design actually needs?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with a live industry debate, plus the ability to reason about a real trade-off rather than giving a one-sided answer.

bullets: Show awareness of the shift toward reusable stock scenery, rented materials, and end-of-run recycling or donation schemes
Acknowledge the tension: some designs genuinely need bespoke, non-reusable builds to achieve their effect
Reason toward a balanced position rather than simply declaring sustainability should always win
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's a real shift happening, more venues are keeping stock scenic pieces they can reuse or repaint, using rental firms for standard flats and platforms instead of building new every time, and building in a plan from the start for where materials go after the run rather than treating a skip as the default ending. I don't think sustainability should be an absolute rule that overrides every design though, because some shows genuinely need a bespoke, non-reusable structure to land their central image, and forcing generic reused pieces onto every production would flatten a lot of good work. I'd want the question asked early in design, not as an afterthought, so sustainable choices get built in from the start rather than bolted on when it's too late to change anything.

commonMistakes: Treating sustainability as a slogan with no practical detail
Ignoring that some designs have genuine, non-negotiable material needs
Refusing to actually take a position on the trade-off when asked
followUps: Can you think of a specific example where reused or stock scenery would genuinely not work?

subtopic: Working at height and harness safety
question: A director wants a performer flown on a harness above the stage for a striking visual moment. As part of the production team, what would concern you and what would you want in place before agreeing to it?
lookingFor: Rigorous safety instinct that treats performer wellbeing as a precondition, not an obstacle to the director's vision.

bullets: Name the core requirement: a qualified flying specialist and properly certified, load-tested equipment, not a general rigger improvising
Insist on extensive rehearsal at low height before it ever goes to full height, plus the performer's own comfort and training
Show willingness to push back on a director's timeline if the safety preparation genuinely isn't ready yet
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first concern would be who's actually rigging and flying that performer, because this needs a specialist flying company or a chartered rigger with harness experience, not a general technician doing their best. I'd want the performer properly trained and comfortable in the harness, with rehearsals starting low to the ground and only building up to full height once everyone, including the performer, is confident, and I'd want that built into the schedule from the start rather than squeezed in during tech week. If the safety preparation wasn't genuinely ready by the date the director wanted it, I think the right thing to do is say so clearly and push the timeline, because a striking visual isn't worth someone getting hurt for the sake of a schedule.

commonMistakes: Focusing only on the visual effect and not the safety preparation behind it
Assuming any rigger can safely fly a performer without specialist experience
Being unwilling to push back on a director's timeline even when safety isn't ready
followUps: What would you do if the director pushed back and said the show had to go on as scheduled anyway?

question: Partway through a run, the production's sponsor pulls out and the budget for the remaining weeks is cut sharply. As part of the production team, how would you approach deciding what changes and what's protected?
lookingFor: Structured priority-setting under real pressure, distinguishing what preserves the show's integrity from what can flex.

bullets: Start by identifying what's essential to the show's safety and its core storytelling versus what's a comfort or a nice-to-have
Show a process: consult the director and heads of department rather than making unilateral cuts
Recognise that some cuts, like reducing crew below a safe minimum, simply aren't on the table regardless of budget
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by drawing a hard line around anything to do with safety, that's not negotiable no matter how tight the budget gets, so crew numbers or maintenance checks wouldn't be where the cuts land. Past that, I'd want to sit down with the director and heads of department together, because what looks like an easy cut to a production manager might quietly gut something the design depends on, so it needs everyone's input rather than one person deciding alone. Realistically I'd be looking at things like reducing rental extras, simplifying a scene change that was always more elaborate than it needed to be, or extending the life of existing stock rather than buying new, protecting the story and the audience's experience as the last thing to touch.

commonMistakes: Suggesting safety-related cuts as an acceptable option
Making the decision unilaterally instead of consulting the wider team
Giving a vague answer with no actual priority order
followUps: What would you do if the director insisted on protecting something you thought was expendable?

question: You're on the book and a fly cue jams halfway through a scene change, leaving the stage half-dressed with the audience watching. What do you do in that moment?
lookingFor: Calm, structured crisis response that prioritises performer and audience safety over saving the moment.

bullets: Prioritise safety first: stop anything that could be dangerous rather than forcing the cue to complete
Communicate immediately and clearly over headset so the whole team knows the state of the stage
Have a fallback instinct, whether that's holding, adapting lighting to cover it, or calling a pause, rather than freezing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The very first thing is safety, if that bar is stuck I'm not forcing it or sending anyone up to force it manually mid-show, because a half-jammed rig with people near it is exactly when accidents happen. I'd call it clearly over headset immediately, everyone needs to know the stage is in a compromised state so lighting and the actors can adapt rather than everyone discovering it separately. Then I'd be thinking about the fastest safe cover, that might mean holding the lighting state to disguise the half-dressed stage while the crew works the problem manually from the ground, or in a worst case calling a brief pause, but the instinct throughout is stay calm and communicate, panic is what actually turns a stuck cue into a real incident.

commonMistakes: Trying to force the mechanism to complete the cue under pressure
Staying silent and hoping it resolves itself instead of communicating immediately
Focusing only on saving the theatrical moment and ignoring the safety risk
followUps: How would you debrief the team afterward to stop it happening again?

subtopic: Discovering a safety fault before opening
question: The day before press night, you notice a piece of rigging hardware looks worn in a way that wasn't flagged in the last inspection. Raising it could delay or even cancel opening. What do you do?
lookingFor: Willingness to prioritise safety over schedule and reputation, with a clear, proportionate process rather than panic or silence.

bullets: State clearly that the concern gets raised immediately, regardless of the pressure of press night
Describe a proportionate process: flag it to the technical manager or rigger, don't just quietly worry about it or fix it yourself
Show understanding that the consequence, a delay, is acceptable and secondary to the risk of not raising it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd raise it immediately, press night or not, because the entire point of noticing something is that it stops being my private worry and becomes the technical manager's decision to inspect properly. I wouldn't try to assess it myself or quietly hope it's fine, I don't have the expertise to make that call, and I also wouldn't just fix it myself without it being properly checked and signed off. If that means press night gets delayed, that's a genuinely acceptable cost, because the alternative is gambling with someone's safety to protect a schedule, and I don't think any production is worth that trade.

commonMistakes: Deciding to stay quiet to avoid delaying opening night
Trying to informally fix or assess it without a qualified person
Treating the delay as the worst possible outcome instead of the safer one
followUps: What would you say to a producer who was furious about the delay?

question: A director under time pressure asks you to skip a scheduled safety check so a technical rehearsal can start on time. How do you handle that?
lookingFor: Confidence to hold a boundary with someone senior when safety is genuinely at stake, delivered constructively rather than as confrontation.

bullets: Be clear that the check happens regardless of pressure, without being unnecessarily combative about it
Offer to find another way to protect the schedule, like running unrelated parts of tech in parallel
Show respect for the director's pressure while still not compromising on the actual safety requirement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd tell the director honestly that I understand the time pressure, but that check isn't something I can skip, it exists precisely for moments when everyone's rushed and might otherwise miss something. I'd try to be useful about it rather than just saying no, so I'd look for another way to protect the schedule, maybe starting with a section of tech that doesn't depend on that particular rig while the check finishes in parallel. I think holding that line respectfully, rather than either caving to the pressure or turning it into a standoff, is what actually earns trust with a director over a longer working relationship.

commonMistakes: Quietly skipping the check to avoid conflict with someone senior
Refusing so bluntly that it damages the working relationship unnecessarily
Not offering any alternative to help the schedule pressure
followUps: What would you do if the director went over your head to get the check skipped anyway?

question: You come up with a striking idea for a scene transition during an informal brainstorm, and a few weeks later a senior designer presents it to the director as their own. What do you do?
lookingFor: Measured self-advocacy that protects the applicant's contribution without being either passive or destructively confrontational.

bullets: Show willingness to address it directly with the person rather than letting resentment build silently
Aim for a private, non-accusatory conversation first rather than escalating immediately
Recognise that if it happened repeatedly or the conversation went nowhere, involving a supervisor becomes reasonable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't just swallow it, but I also wouldn't make a scene about it in front of the director in the moment. I'd go talk to them privately afterward and just be straightforward, something like, I noticed that idea came up when we were talking a few weeks ago, and I wanted to check we're on the same page about it. Most of the time that's actually enough, people genuinely forget where an idea came from in a fast-moving process, but if it kept happening or they brushed me off, I think it would be reasonable to mention it to a supervisor, because being credited for your work is part of actually building a career in this field.

commonMistakes: Saying nothing and letting resentment build silently
Confronting the person publicly or aggressively in the moment
Escalating straight to a supervisor without a private conversation first
followUps: Would your answer change if this were a fellow student rather than someone senior to you?

subtopic: A costume choice flagged as culturally insensitive
question: A cast member privately tells you they're uncomfortable with a costume element that borrows from their culture in a way that feels reductive. What's your first move?
lookingFor: Genuine listening and humility before defensiveness, and understanding that raising this is part of the collaborative process, not an attack on the design.

bullets: Prioritise listening properly and taking the concern seriously rather than becoming defensive about the design
Commit to raising it with the costume designer and director rather than dismissing it or handling it alone
Show understanding that resolving it well usually means genuine dialogue and willingness to change, not just an apology
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first move is to actually listen, properly, without jumping to defend the design or explain why it was intended innocently, because whether it landed well matters more than what anyone meant by it. I'd thank them for telling me, since that takes real courage to raise, and tell them honestly that I'd take it to the costume designer and director rather than trying to quietly smooth it over myself. From there I think it's genuinely their conversation to have too if they want to be part of it, and the resolution should be actual dialogue and a willingness to change the element if needed, not a token apology that leaves the costume exactly as it was.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive about the design instead of listening
Dismissing the concern as oversensitivity
Handling it alone instead of involving the designer and director in a proper conversation
followUps: What would you do if the designer disagreed that there was a problem?

subtopic: Undisclosed use of AI-generated design work
question: You find out a fellow production student submitted AI-generated renderings as their own original design concept for a shared assessment. What's going through your mind, and what do you do?
lookingFor: Clear-eyed reasoning about honesty and craft in a genuinely current grey area, without either overreacting or shrugging it off.

bullets: Distinguish between using AI as a tool in a disclosed, transparent way versus presenting its output as original personal work
Show that the concern is honesty and fairness to the assessment, not a blanket objection to the technology itself
Describe a reasonable next step, like raising it with a tutor, rather than either ignoring it or publicly accusing the student
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What bothers me isn't that they used an AI tool, plenty of designers experiment with generative tools now for early mood images, it's that they presented the output as their own original design thinking on a shared assessment, which isn't honest about where the work actually came from. I think the line is disclosure, if they'd said this started from an AI-generated image and here's how I developed it, that's a legitimate part of a modern design process, but passing it off as unaided original work misrepresents their skill to whoever's grading it and isn't fair to everyone else who did the thinking themselves. I'd raise it privately with a tutor rather than confronting the student myself or letting it slide, because it's really an academic integrity question and not mine to adjudicate.

commonMistakes: Treating any use of AI tools as automatically dishonest
Ignoring the issue because it feels awkward to raise
Publicly accusing the student instead of raising it through a tutor
followUps: Where do you personally think the line should sit for using AI tools in design work?

subtopic: AI in lighting and design workflows
question: AI tools are increasingly used to generate mood boards, previsualise lighting states, and even suggest set designs. What's your view on where these tools genuinely help a production team, and where they fall short?
lookingFor: Informed, balanced engagement with a live industry debate rather than either uncritical enthusiasm or blanket dismissal.

bullets: Name a concrete use case where AI genuinely speeds up early-stage work, like generating quick mood references or previsualising a lighting state
Identify a real limitation, such as AI producing generically plausible ideas that lack the specificity a director's actual vision needs
Land on a balanced view: useful as a starting point or drafting tool, not a substitute for a designer's judgement
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think they're genuinely useful early on, generating a batch of mood images in minutes to spark a conversation with a director, or previsualising a lighting state before you've got expensive rig time, that saves real hours. Where they fall short is that the output tends to be generically plausible rather than specific to the actual story and the actual director's vision, it can look impressive without meaning anything particular. My honest view is that they're a fast way to get a draft or a starting conversation, but the judgement about what a scene actually needs to say still has to come from a person who's read the play closely, so I'd treat it as a tool in the process rather than a replacement for the designer.

commonMistakes: Being uncritically enthusiastic with no mention of limitations
Dismissing the technology entirely with no concrete engagement
Giving a vague opinion with no specific use case named
followUps: Do you think this changes what skills a production student should be learning now?

question: There's growing pressure on the theatre industry to reduce the carbon footprint of touring productions, from haulage to set materials. What do you make of that pressure, and what would you realistically expect a production to change first?
lookingFor: Awareness of a live sustainability debate in the industry, plus realistic, practical thinking rather than idealism with no substance.

bullets: Show awareness that touring haulage, set materials, and energy use for lighting rigs are the biggest contributors
Suggest realistic first changes: routing tours more efficiently, using more energy-efficient LED rigs, building sets designed to be reused or broken down for transport
Acknowledge the tension between environmental pressure and the financial reality touring productions already operate under
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's a genuinely necessary pressure, touring haulage and energy-hungry lighting rigs add up to a real footprint, and the industry can't just treat that as someone else's problem. What I'd expect to change first is probably the easiest wins, more theatres have already been moving to LED lighting rigs because they're cheaper to run as well as greener, and tour routing that groups venues geographically instead of zigzagging the country saves fuel and money at the same time. The harder part is set materials and construction, because building for reuse or easy breakdown often costs more upfront even if it saves money and waste later, and touring productions are usually working on tight margins already, so I think that change needs some structural support, not just goodwill.

commonMistakes: Treating the pressure as purely a marketing concern rather than a real operational issue
Offering only vague good intentions with no concrete first steps
Ignoring the financial tension that makes some changes hard in practice
followUps: Who do you think should be paying for that structural change, venues, producers, or funding bodies?

subtopic: Backstage crew working hours and wellbeing
question: There's been more public conversation recently about long, irregular hours and burnout among backstage and production crew. What's your take on that, and how would you want to see it addressed?
lookingFor: Engaged, informed view on a real industry conversation, with practical suggestions rather than either dismissal or naive idealism.

bullets: Show awareness that production schedules, especially tech week and get-ins, can involve genuinely long, unpredictable hours
Recognise the tension between the industry's project-based, deadline-driven nature and sustainable working conditions
Suggest a realistic direction: better advance scheduling, protected rest periods, and cultural change around treating exhaustion as normal
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've read enough about tech week and get-in schedules to know the hours can be genuinely brutal, long days that run into nights with very little turnaround before the next call, and I think the conversation about that is overdue rather than an overreaction. The hard part is that theatre is inherently deadline-driven, a show has to open on a fixed date whether or not everything's ready, so I don't think the answer is pretending that pressure disappears. What I'd want to see is more realistic advance scheduling that plans for that crunch rather than being surprised by it every time, and protected rest periods that are actually enforced, not just written into a handbook, plus a cultural shift away from treating being permanently exhausted as a badge of honour in this industry.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the issue as just how theatre has always worked
Offering no concrete suggestion for how it could actually be addressed
Ignoring the genuine scheduling constraints that make it a hard problem
followUps: Do you think students should be taught to expect and accept these hours, or push back on them?

question: A number of regional theatres have faced funding cuts in recent years, with knock-on effects on production budgets and staffing. How do you think that pressure changes what's expected of a production team?
lookingFor: Realistic grasp of the funding landscape and its practical effect on how production work actually gets done, not just sympathy without substance.

bullets: Show awareness that funding cuts translate directly into smaller crews, tighter build budgets, and more doubling of roles
Explain the practical effect: production teams have to be more resourceful, reusing stock and simplifying design without losing quality
Avoid blanket pessimism, showing instead that constraint can also sharpen creative problem-solving
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: When funding gets cut, it usually shows up first in smaller crews and tighter build budgets, which means people end up doubling roles that used to be separate, and designs have to lean more on what's already in stock rather than building everything fresh. I think that genuinely changes what's expected of a production team, you need people who are resourceful and can solve a problem with what's available rather than assuming there's budget to buy a solution. I don't think that's purely a loss either, some of the most inventive design work I've read about actually came out of real constraint, so while I think the funding cuts themselves are a serious problem for the sector, I also think production training now probably needs to lean harder into that resourcefulness than it might have needed to a decade ago.

commonMistakes: Treating funding cuts as purely someone else's problem with no effect on the applicant's own training
Offering only pessimism with no mention of how teams actually adapt
Being vague about what specifically changes in day-to-day production work
followUps: What skills do you think become more valuable in a tighter-funded production environment?

question: You're production managing an immersive show where the audience moves freely through the space alongside the performers. Halfway through the run, you realise the crowd flow in one room is getting dangerously congested during a key scene. What do you do?
lookingFor: Practical crisis response for a production-specific safety risk, balancing the artistic design against real audience safety.

bullets: Prioritise safety immediately, treating overcrowding as urgent rather than something to monitor and see
Describe concrete fixes: capacity limits per room, staggered entry, or repositioning stewards, rather than vague reassurance
Show willingness to adjust the show's design if the fix genuinely requires it, in consultation with the director
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd treat that as urgent, not something to keep an eye on and revisit next week, because a congested room with people moving in the dark is exactly how someone gets hurt. The first concrete step would be capping how many audience members can enter that room at once, maybe staggering the group split earlier in the show so they don't all converge on that scene at the same time, and making sure there are stewards actually positioned in that room rather than just at the entrances. If those changes weren't enough, I'd go to the director and be honest that the scene's staging itself might need adjusting, because as much as I'd want to preserve the original design, audience safety isn't something I'd compromise on to protect a directorial choice.

commonMistakes: Treating the congestion as a minor issue to monitor rather than an urgent risk
Offering only vague reassurance with no concrete fix
Refusing to consider adjusting the show's design even if the safety fix required it
followUps: How would you balance that against the director wanting to preserve the exact original staging?
